resources.string: How the brainstem sets the breathing rhythm
A qualitative view of normal quiet breathing. Anatomy and nerve routes are simplified; movement and timing are not to scale.
At the base of the brain, the brainstem connects to the spinal cord. Its lower part, the medulla, contains networks that help drive automatic breathing.
A network of nerve cells in the medulla helps generate recurring bursts of activity for inhalation. The enlarged view highlights the network, not individual nerve connections.
Signals descend from the brainstem to motor neurons in the cervical spinal cord. The phrenic nerves carry those signals to both sides of the diaphragm.
The diaphragm contracts, flattens and moves down. The chest cavity enlarges, the lungs expand, and air flows in.
Quiet exhalation and the next breath
As inspiratory drive fades, the diaphragm relaxes and returns toward its domed shape. Elastic recoil moves air out passively. The next burst begins the cycle again.
